name: Vera Walsh

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for seeing me, Vera. I'm from the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We aren't tied to AI companies, employers, unions or political parties, and everything you tell me stays confidential, so you can say what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. What does a normal working day look like for you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm a carpenter for a regional contractor that builds public buildings, mostly schools and health centres. This year we're putting up a new wing on Ashford Primary, and I'm on the roof structure and the timber cladding outside. Start is seven, I'm on the scaffold most of the day, and I get a lot of satisfaction knowing kids will sit under a roof I built. What wears me out is the paperwork for public jobs, every board has to be signed off three times.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How did you come to the trade?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My dad's a quantity surveyor, so I grew up around sites, but I wanted to build, not count. I did my trade certificate and got taken on at 19, and I've been with the same contractor eight years. My foreman, Pat, is old school and fair, and I'd follow him anywhere.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I live with Ryan, my partner, who's an electrician, and we bought a small house three years ago. Between us we earn well, and we've got about nine months of costs saved on top of the mortgage. We go to church most Sundays, and I coach the under-12 girls' football team on Saturdays. I use an AI app now and then, mainly because the site manager uses one for snag lists, which are the lists of small faults to fix before handover.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Here's the first picture. It's called AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a useful helper for the paperwork and that's about it. On public jobs that's actually welcome, because the sign-offs eat hours. I wouldn't post anything; I'm not one for arguing online.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means work carries on, which suits me. Schools and health centres always need building. The only thing on my mind is my dad, who's 59, because counting and pricing is the sort of thing that software chips away at even in a small way.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep working, keep saving, and stick to our plan to start a family in a couple of years. I'd use the snag list app a bit more since the site manager likes it. I'd tell Dad to keep his head down until he retires.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Our life is on a good track.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to your dad, specifically?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my dad he's got six years left, so be the one who knows the new program better than the young ones. He'd grumble but he'd do it. He's more stubborn than me, which is saying something.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Any money worries at all in this world?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not really. The mortgage is fine, and Ryan's never short of work. We'd like a bigger garden someday, but that's a wish, not a worry.

I'd **stay offline** rather than argue about it.
think: Work carries on because **schools and clinics** always need building.
Her **dad's pricing work** could be chipped at, which crosses her mind.
do: Keep **working and saving** with her partner Ryan.
Start a **family** in a couple of years as planned.
Use the **snag list app** a little more.
feel: **Calm**, feeling their life is on track.
S0.quote: I'd tell my dad he's got six years left, so be the one who knows the new program better than the young ones.
fieldNote: Her one AI concern is for her **father**, not herself.
The **two-trade household** feels secure in this world.
She values **loyalty** to her foreman and firm.

steps.text: Keep building the roof on the Ashford Primary school wing
Start a family with Ryan in about two years
Use the site manager's snag-list app more often

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say trades are lucky, we've still got work, but office folk need help. At church I'd say we should look out for families where someone loses an office job. I'd say people should learn a trade instead of waiting for government to fix it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, my job's fine for now, but my dad's job is right in the path. Pricing and checking drawings is what this takes over. I'd also think the public contracts might get tighter, because the council's planners and buyers will use AI to squeeze prices.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep working and learn whatever app the site uses once Pat's tried it. I'd help Dad think about early retirement or moving into site inspection, which is more hands-on. Ryan and I would keep the family plans but save a bit more, maybe an extra two hundred a month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Not for me, but for Dad, and a bit for what the contracts will look like.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why wait for Pat to try the app first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because Pat doesn't fall for nonsense. If he says it's worth it, it's worth it. I'm not against new things, I just don't jump first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would a tighter contract mean for you on site?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Less time on each job, more pressure to finish fast, and maybe fewer of us on a crew. It wouldn't take my job, but it might take my overtime. Overtime is our holiday money.

steps.text: Learn the site's new app once foreman Pat approves it

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's going too fast, and families need to come first. At church I'd say we pull together and look after each other. At work I'd tell people to keep their savings close.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means both me and Ryan have hands-on jobs that could go by 2031, when I'm 32. I think public buildings would be the last to let robots in, because of all the sign-offs, so maybe we've a bit longer. But it's realistic that our incomes shrink within five years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd pay down the mortgage faster, maybe five hundred extra a month, so we're not stuck. I'd ask the firm about training in robot supervision on public sites, since those jobs will need a human sign-off. We'd still try for our first child, but maybe sooner, while we're both earning.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but I'd hold it together. I'm not one to fall apart.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd have a child sooner, not later. Why?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because I'd rather have a baby while we've both got good pay than wait and hope. My mum always says there's never a perfect time. I'd trust God and our savings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you blame if this happened?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The tech companies and the governments that didn't slow it down. But I wouldn't expect a handout either. I'd expect to work and look after my own family.

I'd tell people at work to keep their **savings close**.

fieldNote: She sees public sector **sign-off rules** as a buffer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say there's time to get ready if we're sensible. At church I'd say the same: plan, don't panic. I'd tell the girls on my football team to learn a skill that robots can't easily copy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: With robots around 2034, I'd be 35, Ryan 36, and we'd have a toddler. Public jobs might keep humans a bit longer. I'd feel uneasy, but it's manageable.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep working, pay down the mortgage a bit faster, and have our first child as planned. In 2030 I'd ask about supervision training on public sites. We'd keep a year of costs saved.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but steady.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What skill would you tell the girls to learn?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Something with people, like nursing or teaching, or something where you're in charge of machines, not doing the same job as them. I'd also tell them to save from their first paycheck. Dad told me that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you consider leaving construction?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not unless I had to. I like building schools. If the robots come, I want to be the one checking them.

I'd tell the football girls to learn **skills robots can't copy**.

**Public jobs** might keep humans longer, making it manageable.
do: Pay down the **mortgage** a bit faster.
S3.quote: If the robots come, I want to be the one checking them.
fieldNote: She sees **supervising robots** as her natural next step.
Her advice to young girls reflects **family values** about saving.
More warning lets her keep plans **on schedule**.

steps.text: Pay down the house mortgage a bit faster

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fifth and last picture is called AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is enough to plan properly. I'd tell people at work and church not to worry yet, just be wise. Nothing changes overnight.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: By 2039 I'd be 40 with kids at school and the house mostly paid. I'd hope to be running a crew by then. I'd still be a bit uneasy, because supervising is the thinking part that changes first, in 2036.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep working, become a foreman by my mid-thirties, have the family we want. I'd learn new tools when Pat and the firm bring them in. I'd keep saving steadily, nothing dramatic.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but mostly settled.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You noticed the supervising part changes first. How would you handle that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd make sure I'm the foreman who knows both the timber and the machines. If AI does the scheduling, fine, but someone still has to stand on the roof and say this isn't right. I'd want to be that person.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want for your own kids?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A trade or something solid, and faith and family around them. I'd want them to work hard and not expect anyone to hand them a living. Same as my parents wanted for me.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because Ryan and I both work with our hands and we'd want a family just then. What would help is apprenticeships and training in supervising robots, and the government making public sites keep a qualified person in charge.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: About community. When the mill closed in my grandad's town, it was the church and neighbours who held people together. I'd want people to remember that before they start looking for someone to blame.

headlineQuote: When the mill closed in my grandad's town, it was the church and neighbours who held people together.
portrait: Vera is a **27-year-old carpenter** building school and health centre roofs for a regional contractor.
She and her electrician partner **Ryan** own a small house and have nine months saved.
She's **calm** in AI Plateau and uneasy in Steady Disruption, mostly for her quantity surveyor father.
AGI by 2028 makes her **anxious**: both jobs are exposed, so she'd overpay the mortgage.
She adopts tools **once proven**, values faith and family, and wants to supervise robots.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because both she and Ryan work with their hands and want a family.
whatWouldHelp: **Robot supervision training** and rules keeping a qualified person in charge of public sites.
